standard.title: Celebrations and commemorations
standard.description: the celebrations and commemorations of significant events shared with their families and others
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have lived experience of family celebrations. No formal prior HASS curriculum.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify celebrations and commemorations that are significant to their families and communities, and explain why they are important.

nodes.label: What celebrations and commemorations are
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a celebration (marking a joyful or important event) and a commemoration (remembering a significant person or event), and name examples of each from their own experience.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least one celebration and one commemoration from their own life and describe what happens during it.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of celebrations (birthdays, religious festivals, cultural events) and commemorations (Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week) from a provided calendar; describe key features of each type.
wider: Compare how different cultural and religious groups celebrate similar occasions in different ways; for example, how New Year is celebrated in different cultures
Explore the role of First Nations Australian celebrations and commemorations, such as NAIDOC Week and Coming of the Light, in maintaining cultural identity
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish celebration from commemoration cannot explain why events are significant — the conceptual distinction underpins the next node's explanatory demand.

response_modes.reason: The celebration/commemoration distinction is conceptually subtle at Foundation level. Use concrete examples and visual anchors — what does each look like, how do people feel, what are they marking?

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The diversity of celebrations in a Foundation class (religious, cultural, national, family) provides rich opportunity to explore why different groups mark different events and what this reveals about identity and community.
success_criteria: Names at least one celebration and one commemoration from their own experience
Describes at least one feature of each (what happens, who participates)

nodes.label: Why celebrations and commemorations are important
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why at least one celebration or commemoration is important to their family or community, using language about significance, memory, and belonging.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain in their own words why one celebration or commemoration matters to them or their family.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss why multiple celebrations and commemorations are important to different people and groups; connect significance to ideas of memory, identity, tradition and shared belonging.
wider: Explore how generations hand on traditions through celebrations and what would be lost if they stopped
Investigate how First Nations Australian ceremonies and storytelling transmit cultural knowledge from one generation to the next

response_modes.reason: Significance is most accessible when students discuss their own celebrations first, then encounter others'. Use sharing circles and a class calendar to build range.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Students explaining why their own celebrations matter, then listening to others, builds genuine cross-cultural understanding — this is one of the richest widening opportunities in the Foundation curriculum.
success_criteria: Explains why at least one celebration or commemoration is important to them or their family
Uses at least one term relating to significance, memory or belonging
